title: Copy-on-write (CoW)
summary: Copying an array is cheap because Swift only really copies the data when one of the copies is changed.
body: **In simple words:** Arrays can be huge. If every `let b = a` copied a million elements, Swift would be slow. So `Array`, `Dictionary`, `Set` and `String` share the same storage after a copy, and only make a real copy at the moment someone **writes** to a shared one.
**Real-life analogy:** Two students share one textbook. Nobody buys a second book until one of them wants to write notes in it. Then that student gets their own copy.

**How it works:** the array struct holds a pointer to a heap buffer. Before a mutation it checks "am I the only owner of this buffer?" (`isKnownUniquelyReferenced`). If yes, it changes in place. If no, it copies the buffer first, then changes its own copy.

**Important:** CoW is **not automatic** for your own structs. A plain struct copies all its fields every time. If you build a big custom value type, you can add CoW yourself by keeping storage in a private class and checking uniqueness before writes.
**Hidden cost:** if you accidentally keep a second reference to an array while mutating it in a loop, every mutation may copy the whole array, turning O(n) work into O(n²).
keyPoints: Standard collections share storage on copy and copy only on the first write to a shared buffer.
Your own structs do not get CoW for free; implement it for large value types.
Use `dict[key, default: []].append(x)` to mutate in place instead of read-modify-write patterns that create copies.

mistakes: Believing every struct uses CoW automatically.
Thinking CoW makes sharing a `var` between threads safe - it does not; it is still a data race.
followups: **Is copying an Array O(1) or O(n)?** O(1) to copy; O(n) when the first write happens on a shared buffer.
**How would you make a custom struct CoW?** Private final class storage + `isKnownUniquelyReferenced` check in every mutating path.
